The Defenseman. The primary position responsible for preventing the opposing team from scoring in ice hockey.

Typically, each team fields two defensemen at a time, positioned alongside a goaltender to block shots, check opposing forwards, and initiate counterattacks. The position evolved from purely defensive specialist work in early hockey into a dynamic role demanding both physical prowess and skating artistry.

Defensemen traditionally wear jersey numbers 1 through 3, though modern numbering has become more flexible. They typically don blue jerseys on one team and red on the other. Early hockey defensemen were purely defensive specialists, often lacking the skating ability or offensive skill of forwards. Bobby Orr shattered this archetype in the nineteen-sixties and nineteen-seventies by combining elite defensive positioning with offensive contributions, actively joining rushes.

The position fundamentally changed with Orr's arrival. There's the "staying at home" defenseman who focuses on defense and clearing duties, and the "rushing" defenseman who initiates attacks from the blue line—a style popularized by Orr. Eddie Shore exemplified the bruising defenseman of an earlier era, using physical intimidation and checking to control the ice and protect his goal.

Modern defensemen require exceptional skating ability, hockey sense, positioning, and physical conditioning to compete at the NHL level. The transition from passive defense to active puck involvement represents one of the sport's most significant positional evolutions. Defensemen typically play in pairs—a "shut-down" defenseman focusing on defense against opposing top lines and a "point" defenseman playing from the blue line to facilitate offense.

The position must master skills like stick-checking, using the stick to separate the puck from an opponent, body positioning, and shot-blocking to protect the goaltender. Modern defensemen are expected to contribute offensively by maintaining possession, generating assists, and controlling play from the blue line, expanding their role significantly. The defenseman's role expanded to include penalty-killing duties and power-play participation, making it a more comprehensive position than in hockey's early decades.
